https://www.dw.com/en/slovakia-pm-robert.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5N6CI 'I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,' said Slovak PM Robert Fico Image: Martin Baumann/TASR/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement "I'm afraid of war," Robert Fico told medical students at a teaching hospital in Presov last week. "What is happening in Europe today, what we're hearing and seeing today, is that the military conflict in Ukraine has got out of control," he went on, warning them that Europe faced the possibility of a wider war. He asked the students to imagine Slovakia being told to prepare "5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers" who would go somewhere to fight "without us even knowing whom they are fighting, or why, or what for." Then he turned to Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty , under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. "I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5," Fico said. "Yes, we are in NATO . We value that. Cooperation and fulfilling our obligations matter to us. But as prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict." Czech President Petr Pavel has questioned whether Fico understands the meaning of the word 'solidarity' Image: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO The remarks prompted uproar from the Slovak opposition and also a spat with Petr Pavel , president of neighboring Czechia and former chairman of NATO's Military Committee. "If anyone says they're glad to be a member of NATO … but are unwilling to get involved if anyone else is attacked, then they have not understood the word solidarity," Pavel said. Fico replied that he understood that Pavel, as a former NATO general, would like to fight, while he himself preferred peace. The impact on Slovakia's standing The Slovak prime minister's fear of a wider war is shared by many Europeans. But critics at home gave his remarks short shrift. "Isn't he a prime minister? Isn't he the leader of a country? Is he not supposed to lead people instead of expressing fears?" asked former Slovak Foreign Minister Miro Wlachovsky, now a distinguished fellow at the GLOBSEC think tank. Slovak PM Robert Fico (left) and Czech PM Andrej Babis (right) have both stressed their preference for diplomacy when it comes to ending the war in Ukraine Image: Jaroslav Ozana/CTK/picture alliance "My question for him as prime minister is: OK, even if the situation is as bad as you are saying, what I want to hear from you is how the country is prepared. What have you done for preparedness? Who will come to our aid in case we are attacked?" Wlachovsky told DW. Asked whether Fico's remarks could damage Slovakia's standing among its allies, Wlachovsky replied: "It's already done." Political background to Fico's comments Analysts see a clear political context to Fico's remarks. The Slovak prime minister will face a difficult reelection fight next year. Some observers believe Fico is trying to steal votes from the extreme-right Republika party, which is viscerally hostile to NATO and the EU and opposes military support for Ukraine. Wlachovsky compared Fico's rhetoric to that of Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban and the current Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis , both of whom have presented themselves as the candidates of peace. Babis was heavily criticized during his unsuccessful 2023 presidential campaign after questioning during a televised debate whether the Czech Republic should send troops to NATO ally Poland if it came under attack. What is NATO's Article 5? Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former NATO spokesperson, told DW that Article 5 was "the most solemn pledge that a country can make to another." But its central purpose, she said, was deterrence: convincing a potential aggressor that it would face the alliance together, rather than an isolated member. "This is about solidarity, standing together, underpinning deterrence and therefore avoiding war," she said. "NATO is a defensive alliance. It's not an offensive alliance." Nor would invoking Article 5 automatically send every member's troops into combat, she said. The North Atlantic Council, where every ally is represented, would assess an attack and decide by consensus whether it constituted an Article 5 situation — Slovakia's voice would be equal to that of its 31 partners in that room, she said. Once consensus was reached, each country would then assist the attacked ally by taking the action it deemed necessary, which might — or might not — involve armed force. Article 5 has been invoked only once, following the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States. Lungescu pointed to one of NATO's initial responses: sending AWACS surveillance aircraft to patrol US skies and help prevent another attack. Solidarity: Slovakia's neighbors and NATO allies Poland and Czechia in 2022 pledged to protect Slovak airspace. Image: Petr David Josek/AP/dpa/picture alliance She pointed out that Slovakia already benefits from the same solidarity Fico appeared to question. The country hosts a NATO multinational battlegroup established after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with personnel from several allies alongside Slovak troops. Its purpose is to deter an attack on Slovakia. 'Exactly what Putin wants' For former Slovak Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad, the danger lies in allowing that fear to dictate policy towards Ukraine. "This is exactly what Vladimir Putin wants," said Nad, who was defense minister from 2020 to 2023 and is now head of the non-parliamentary opposition Democrats party. "He wants citizens in the EU and NATO to believe that if EU and NATO countries continue to support Ukraine, this escalatory situation might lead to a Third World War or something like that," Nad told DW. Nad was in office when Slovakia decided to hand over its entire fleet of ageing MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine . Fico's government later sought a criminal investigation into the transfer; prosecutors closed the case, finding no crime. "Even when I was defense minister, I heard this not only from ordinary people but also from some ministers around the table: that we shouldn't help Ukraine with this or that equipment or capability or ammunition, because it might create a difficult situation in terms of escalation towards Russia," he went on. "None of that happened." Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan Could Slovakia replace Hungary as EU's main disruptor? https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A man stands at the site of his parents' house, destroyed during a Russian airstrike Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen A man stands at the site of his parents' house, destroyed during a Russian airstrike Photograph: Reuters Ukraine Russia and Ukraine resume energy strikes despite Trump warnings Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries Europe live – latest updates Andrew Roth in Kyiv Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.14 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump . Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to . Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”. Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed. In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six. “The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics ⁠facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement. View image in fullscreen Wreckage of a Russian jet-powered drone lies inside a crater that appeared at the site of a residential area after a strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals. What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine? Read more “It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in his social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration. “Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.” Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations. But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine. The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers also complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines. The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes that his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said that Ukraine should “get a new president”. Asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said. Musk, the powerful head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a top critic of Zelenskyy in the US. On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe US foreign policy Donald Trump news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
